newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia property market seen softening.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia property market seen softening.

text.p: Malaysia's property market is expected to soften further this year after a general decline in 1996, with a "slight glut" forecast in office space, the government announced on Tuesday.
Property transactions rose 23 percent in value to 49 billion ringgit ($20 billion) last year, the Valuation and Property Services Department said in its Property Market Report 1996.
But the growth was lower than the 34 percent jump in 1995, when transactions reached almost 40 billion ringgit, said the department, which is part of the finance ministry.
"The market is bullish but some further consolidation could be seen this year," Deputy Finance Minister Affifuddin Omar told reporters.
"There would be a slight glut in office space. The department would like to tell developers that if you keep on building, you may not be able to sell," Affifuddin said.
Officials said 270,548 property deals were done in 1996, compared to 251,546 in 1995.
A slowdown was already evident this year, with the number of deals falling about eight percent in the first two months to 40,225, from 43,612 in the same period of 1996, the officials said.
They said commercial properties, including office buildings, have been showing poor demand, with the number of transactions dropping 6.3 percent last year from 1995.
The officials estimated that Kuala Lumpur will have 2.03 million square metres of new office space by 1999, bringing the total to about 5.6 million square metres.
There was no estimate on occupancy, but officials doubted that demand could match the projected supply.

"The new government centre Putrajaya will be up by 1998, and could also take away some demand for office space in Kuala Lumpur," said Sahadi Bahari, director-general of the valuation and property services department.
Putrajaya, being built on 4,400 hectres (11,000 acres) of land 35 km (22 miles) south of Kuala Lumpur, is estimated to cost 20 billion ringgit.
Around 76,000 civil servants and 59,000 private sector employees will work in the new federal administrative capital, said officials.

Affifuddin said the residential sector was the most vibrant portion of the market and was expected to retain its lead. The sector commanded 63 percent of the deals and 38 percent of the sales value in 1996.
"The government fully realises the desire of every Malaysian to own his home and is giving priority to this," he said.
To curb speculation on private homes and control prices, the government had to restrict buying by foreigners and introduced property gains taxes last year, said Affifuddin.
But he added: "Our policy is not direct intervention. It is up to the market to equilibrate itself."
He said the finance ministry was concerned that loans extended by financial institutions to property buyers could fuel inflation if not controlled.
He said lending to property buyers amounted to 25.3 percent of the total loans last year.
"Twenty-five percent is considered quite a high exposure," he said.
